items.title: Realification of a complex vector space by restriction of scalars
Complexification as $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$ with its canonical real-linear embedding
The direct-sum model $V\oplus iV$ of a complexification
Complexification of a real-linear map
Conjugations and real structures on a complex vector space
The fixed real form of a conjugation
The tensor and direct-sum models of complexification are canonically complex-linearly isomorphic
items.strategy: Send $z\otimes v$ to the formal vector $zv$ in $V\oplus iV$, verify well-definedness from the tensor universal property, and recover the inverse from the canonical embedding of $V$ and the complex scalar action.

items.title: Complexification is initial for real-linear maps into complex vector spaces, and is unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: For a real-linear map $f:V\to W$, define the factor on $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V$ by $(a+bi)\otimes v\mapsto af(v)+ibf(v)$ and use the tensor universal property. Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism is the standard representing-object argument.

items.title: Complexification is a functor on real vector spaces and real-linear maps
items.strategy: Define $T_{\mathbb C}=1\otimes T$ on elementary tensors, and check the identity and composition laws on generators using tensor functoriality.

items.title: Complexification preserves kernels, images, finite rank, nullity, and short exact sequences
items.strategy: Pass to the direct-sum model, where $T_{\mathbb C}(v+iw)=Tv+iTw$ acts componentwise. Kernels, images, dimensions, and exactness then reduce to the corresponding real statements on each coordinate.

items.title: A real basis becomes a complex basis after complexification, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}V)=\dim_{\mathbb R}V$
items.strategy: Apply the tensor-product basis theorem to the real basis of $V$ and the basis $1,i$ of $\mathbb C$, then use the direct-sum model to show that the embedded real basis vectors alone already form a complex basis.

items.title: Realification doubles finite dimension
items.strategy: If $(e_j)$ is a complex basis, prove over $\mathbb R$ that $e_1,ie_1,\dots,e_n,ie_n$ span the realification and remain independent by separating real and imaginary coefficients.

items.title: The fixed points of a conjugation form a real vector space whose complexification recovers the ambient complex space
items.strategy: Show the fixed set is closed under real scalars. For $v$, split it as $(v+\sigma v)/2+i\,(v-\sigma v)/(2i)$ to obtain fixed vectors giving surjectivity from the fixed-point complexification, and use the standard embedding argument for injectivity.

items.title: Real forms of a complex vector space correspond exactly to conjugations
items.strategy: From a real form take the canonical conjugation on its complexification; from a conjugation take the fixed real form and use the reconstruction theorem to identify the original complex space with its complexification.

items.title: A complex-linear operator comes from a real operator exactly when it commutes with the chosen conjugation
items.strategy: A complexified real operator obviously commutes with canonical conjugation on elementary tensors. Conversely, restriction to the fixed real form is well defined for a commuting operator, and the reconstruction theorem shows that its complexification recovers the original map.

items.title: Complexification preserves the characteristic and minimal polynomials of a finite-dimensional real operator
items.strategy: Use a real basis and its complexified basis to see that $T$ and $T_{\mathbb C}$ have the same matrix, hence the same characteristic polynomial. The minimal polynomial is then unchanged by the published field-extension lemma.

items.title: For a real operator, nonreal generalised eigenspaces of the complexification occur in conjugate pairs
items.strategy: If $\sigma$ is canonical conjugation, then $\sigma\,(T_{\mathbb C}-\lambda I)^e=(T_{\mathbb C}-\overline\lambda I)^e\sigma$. Therefore $\sigma$ carries $\ker(T_{\mathbb C}-\lambda I)^e$ anti-linearly onto $\ker(T_{\mathbb C}-\overline\lambda I)^e$.

items.title: A nonreal eigenvector yields an invariant real two-plane and the standard rotation-scaling block
items.strategy: Write a nonreal eigenvector as $u+iv$ with $u,v$ in the fixed real form. Comparing real and imaginary parts of $(T-a-bi)(u+iv)=0$ gives the invariant plane and its matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a&-b\\ b&a\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $b\ne0$.

title: Complexification, Realification and Real Structures: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The standard embedding $\mathbb R^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^n$ is the canonical complexification map
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathbb C^n$ by sending $z\otimes e_j$ to the $j$th standard vector scaled by $z$, and track the real basis vectors under the canonical embedding.

items.title: Complexifying a real polynomial space gives the same degree bound with complex coefficients
items.strategy: Write a complexified polynomial as $p+iq$ with $p,q$ real and check directly that the universal map identifies $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}$ with $\mathbb C[x]_{\le d}$.

items.title: Realifying $\mathbb C^n$ gives $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with basis $e_1,ie_1,\dots,e_n,ie_n$
items.strategy: Start from the standard complex basis of $\mathbb C^n$, rewrite every vector in real and imaginary parts, and verify real linear independence of the doubled basis.

items.title: The real quarter-turn diagonalises after complexification but has no real eigenvector
items.strategy: For the matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, compute the eigenvalues $\pm i$ over $\mathbb C$, diagonalise there, and compare with the absence of real roots of $x^2+1$.

items.title: One nonreal eigenvector reconstructs the invariant real plane of a rotation-scaling block
items.strategy: Take an eigenvector $u+iv$ for $a+bi$ with $b\ne0$, pass to real and imaginary parts, and display the real $2\times2$ block on $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{u,v\}$.

items.title: Different conjugations on $\mathbb C^2$ can have different fixed real forms
items.strategy: Compare coordinatewise complex conjugation with a conjugation twisted by a complex-linear involution, and compute the two fixed real subspaces explicitly.

items.title: A complex-linear map need not preserve a chosen real form
items.strategy: Choose a fixed conjugation on $\mathbb C^2$ and a complex-linear operator that does not commute with it; the descent criterion then shows that the map does not come from the fixed real form.

items.title: FALSE: complexification doubles finite dimension
items.strategy: Refute the claim with $\mathbb R^n$, whose complexification is $\mathbb C^n$ and therefore has the same numerical dimension over its new scalar field.

items.title: FALSE: every complex vector space has a preferred real form
items.strategy: Use one complex vector space with two distinct conjugations and compare their fixed subspaces. The difference shows that a real form is extra structure, not canonical data.

items.title: FALSE: every complex-linear operator descends to every chosen real form
items.strategy: Use a chosen conjugation and an operator that fails to commute with it. The descent criterion isolates the missing hypothesis exactly.

items.title: FALSE: complexification creates a real eigenvector whenever it creates a complex one
items.strategy: The quarter-turn on $\mathbb R^2$ gains the eigenvalues $\pm i$ after complexification but still has no real eigenvector, so the real and complex eigenvalue questions are different.

title: Exterior Powers, Orientation and Hodge Duality

items.title: Alternating $k$-linear maps
The $k$th exterior power as the tensor-power quotient by repeated-vector relations
Decomposable $k$-vectors and the basic wedge product
The graded exterior algebra $\Lambda V$
The induced map $\Lambda^kT$ on exterior powers
Orientation of a finite-dimensional real vector space
Exterior powers represent alternating multilinear maps and are unique up to unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Factor an alternating $k$-linear map through the tensor power, note that the repeated-vector relations lie in its kernel, and pass to the quotient. Uniqueness is the usual representing-object argument.

items.title: The basic wedge map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k$ is multilinear and alternating
items.strategy: Because the wedge is the image of the universal tensor map under a quotient, multilinearity is inherited from tensors and alternation is forced by the repeated-vector relations.

items.title: Increasing-index wedges of a basis form a basis of $\Lambda^kV$
items.strategy: Start from the tensor-product basis, use alternation to rewrite every wedge into increasing order, and prove independence by evaluating against alternating coordinate forms.

items.title: If $\dim V=n$, then $\dim\Lambda^kV=\binom{n}{k}$
items.strategy: The basis theorem indexes a basis of $\Lambda^kV$ by the $k$-element subsets of an ordered basis of $V$, so the dimension is the resulting count.

items.title: If $k>\dim V$, then $\Lambda^kV=0$
items.strategy: When $k$ exceeds the basis size, there are no increasing $k$-tuples, so the basis theorem leaves no nonzero basis wedges.

items.title: A decomposable wedge is nonzero exactly when its vectors are linearly independent
items.strategy: Dependent vectors give a repeated direction after solving one vector in terms of the others, so alternation kills the wedge. For independent vectors, extend to a basis and observe that the wedge is one of the basis vectors from the preceding theorem.

items.title: Exterior multiplication is well defined, graded, associative, unital, and graded-commutative
items.strategy: Define products on decomposable wedges by concatenation, descend from the tensor algebra, and compute the sign of block swaps. In characteristic two, formulate the law through alternation rather than a sign cancellation that becomes vacuous.

items.title: Exterior powers are functorial
items.strategy: Use the induced tensor map on the quotient, then check the identity and composition laws on decomposable wedges and lift them to the whole exterior power.

items.title: In basis-wedge coordinates, the matrix of $\Lambda^kT$ is the signed matrix of $k$-minors
items.strategy: Expand $T(e_{j_1})\wedge\cdots\wedge T(e_{j_k})$ in the wedge basis and collect coefficients. Multilinearity and alternation leave exactly the determinant of each $k\times k$ submatrix.

items.title: On $\Lambda^{n}V$, the induced map $\Lambda^{n}T$ is multiplication by $\det T$
items.strategy: When $k=n$, the exterior power is one-dimensional with basis the wedge of an ordered basis, and the signed-minor matrix has the single entry $\det T$.

items.title: Determinant multiplicativity follows from the top exterior power
items.strategy: Compare $\Lambda^n(S\circ T)$ with $\Lambda^nS\circ\Lambda^nT$ on the one-dimensional space $\Lambda^nV$ and read off the two resulting scalars.

items.title: A real linear isomorphism preserves or reverses orientation according to the sign of its determinant
items.strategy: Track one positively oriented basis through the map. The top exterior action multiplies its oriented volume element by $\det T$, so the sign decides whether the transported basis remains in the chosen orientation class.

items.title: The Gram inner product on $\Lambda^kV$
The Gram formula gives a well-defined positive-definite inner product on exterior powers, and $\|v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k\|^2$ is the Gram determinant
items.strategy: Define the pairing on decomposable wedges by the determinant of the Gram matrix, descend it through the quotient, and use the Gram-determinant criterion together with the basis theorem to prove positivity and the independence test.

items.title: The oriented unit volume form
The Hodge star on an oriented finite-dimensional real inner-product space
The Hodge star exists uniquely and is given by the complementary-basis formula in an oriented orthonormal basis
items.strategy: For fixed degree $k$, represent the functional $\beta\mapsto \alpha\wedge\beta$ against the one-dimensional top exterior power using the Gram inner product and the chosen unit volume form. In an oriented orthonormal basis, compute the image of each basis wedge by the complementary index set and its permutation sign.

items.title: The Hodge star is an isometry and satisfies $\star^2=(-1)^{k(n-k)}$ on $\Lambda^kV$
items.strategy: Apply the orthonormal-basis formula twice. The same basis calculation shows that $\star$ permutes an orthonormal basis up to sign, so it preserves the Gram inner product.

items.title: Interior product on the exterior algebra
Interior product is the adjoint of exterior multiplication by a vector
items.strategy: For each $v$, exterior multiplication by $v$ is a linear map $\Lambda^kV\to\Lambda^{k+1}V$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, so it has a unique adjoint. Compute that adjoint on decomposable basis wedges and identify it with contraction by $v$.

items.title: Exterior multiplication and interior product satisfy the graded anticommutation identity
items.strategy: Verify the identity on decomposable wedges by separating whether the contracted vector already appears. Extend by linearity and use the adjoint characterization to keep the sign bookkeeping honest.

items.title: In oriented Euclidean three-space, the cross product is $\star(u\wedge v)$
items.strategy: Using the standard coordinate cross-product formula in an oriented orthonormal basis, verify directly that both constructions are bilinear, alternating, orthogonal to the input vectors, and have the same oriented unit-basis values. The uniqueness forced by those properties identifies them.

title: Exterior Powers, Orientation and Hodge Duality: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Bases and dimensions of exterior powers of $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^3$, and $\mathbb R^4$
items.strategy: List the increasing-index wedge bases explicitly and count them degree by degree to match the dimension formula and the vanishing above top degree.

items.title: A wedge product detects linear dependence in concrete coordinates
items.strategy: Compute a few sample wedges in low dimension and compare the zero and nonzero cases with the linear-independence criterion.

items.title: All exterior powers of a diagonal operator are diagonal
items.strategy: Apply the functoriality and minor-matrix theorem to a diagonal matrix and read the diagonal entries as the products of the chosen eigenvalues.

items.title: A concrete second exterior-power matrix matches the signed $2\times2$ minors
items.strategy: Choose one non-diagonal matrix, compute $\Lambda^2T$ on the wedge basis directly, and compare each coefficient with the corresponding signed minor.

items.title: Oriented area and volume are recovered from wedges and Gram determinants
items.strategy: Compute the norm squares of sample wedges from their Gram matrices and compare them with the familiar squared area or volume formulas.

items.title: The Hodge star in dimensions two, three, and four
items.strategy: Write the star of each basis wedge in oriented orthonormal coordinates and check the square and norm formulas degree by degree.

items.title: The cross product is recovered from $\star(u\wedge v)$ in $\mathbb R^3$
items.strategy: Compute $u\wedge v$, apply the Hodge star, and compare with the coordinate cross-product formula on a few sample pairs.

items.title: Reversing orientation negates the Hodge star while keeping the metric fixed
items.strategy: Compare the oriented unit volume form and Hodge star for two opposite orientations on the same Euclidean space and compute the sign change on basis wedges.

items.title: A bivector in $\mathbb R^4$ need not be decomposable
items.strategy: Use a sum such as $e_1\wedge e_2+e_3\wedge e_4$, wedge it with itself, and show the result cannot vanish as it would for a decomposable bivector.

items.title: FALSE: $\Lambda^kV$ is canonically a subspace of $V^{\otimes k}$ over every field
items.strategy: The exterior power is defined as a quotient of the tensor power. Show that the quotient map need not admit a canonical splitting, so without extra structure there is no preferred subspace realizing $\Lambda^kV$ inside $V^{\otimes k}$.

items.title: FALSE: an inner product determines an orientation
items.strategy: On one Euclidean space, exhibit the two opposite orientations with the same metric. The Hodge-star example makes the difference visible while the inner product stays fixed.

items.title: FALSE: an orientation determines an inner product
items.strategy: Keep one orientation on $\mathbb R^n$ and compare two distinct positive-definite inner products. Their Gram norms and Hodge stars differ, so orientation alone is insufficient.

items.title: FALSE: Hodge star needs only the vector-space structure
items.strategy: Compare the stars arising from different orientations or different inner products on the same underlying vector space. The operator changes, so it is not purely linear-algebraic without metric and orientation data.
